The shade of hell does not clarify the worldly garden parable.
Water from heaven brings forth vegetation, grain, palms, and grape gardens, directly grounding their fertility in divine agency.
Gardens, palms, crops, and varied fruit are divine provision whose harvest carries an ethical claim.
God spreads the earth and places rivers, fruits, and grape gardens within its ordered design.
Rain provides drink and pasture, supplying the prior condition for the cultivated abundance in the parable.
Palms and grapes are presented as divinely supplied provision and a sign for those who understand.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope.
Worldly splendour is explicitly apportioned as a trial, directly clarifying the garden owner's test.
Good and evil are both forms of trial, supplying the general test framework for bestowed abundance.
Rain makes the earth green, a compact parallel to divinely renewed cultivation.
Water is sent down in measure and lodged in the earth, directly supplying the garden's sustaining condition.
Gardens and springs are questioned as possessions that cannot be assumed permanent.
Gardens, springs, crops, and palm trees form the very abundance whose security is challenged.
The crop and fruiting palm image closely parallels the garden's ordered agricultural plenty.
Heavenly water brings forth beautiful gardens that humans cannot independently make grow.
Whatever worldly goods and adornment are given remain temporary beside what is with God.
Those who see worldly splendour envy it, exposing the visual allure behind the owner's boast.
Those given knowledge answer the desire for splendour by preferring God's lasting reward.
Dead land revived for food establishes the divine life-giving source of cultivated produce.
The fruits and the work of human hands call for gratitude rather than possessive self-confidence.
Material houses and adornments could be universally granted to unbelievers, showing that such abundance is not a mark of true worth.
Gold ornament is only enjoyment of worldly life, while the Hereafter belongs with the Lord.
The question about what people sow prepares the denial of independent human control over cultivation.
God can reduce a crop to dry debris, closely paralleling the threatened reversal of the garden.
Worldly life is adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth and children, like vegetation that flourishes and then becomes debris.
Wealth and children are explicitly a trial, directly explaining the moral pressure of the garden owner's riches.
Water can sink beyond reach, directly paralleling the warning that the garden's water may disappear.
The owners of a garden are explicitly tested, making this the closest external narrative parallel.
Their resolve to harvest the garden privately begins a direct counterpart about possessive control of abundance.
A divine visitation strikes the garden while its owners are unaware, showing provision's vulnerability.
The garden is reduced to a scorched field, closely paralleling the threatened ruin in the two-gardens parable.
The owners call one another early to take possession of the harvest, displaying their planned control over it.
Their urgency to harvest shows dependence on a prosperity they wrongly presume secure.
They proceed quietly toward the garden, intensifying their attempt to control its benefit.
They plan to exclude the needy from the garden's produce, giving the wealth episode an ethical counterpart.
They go with firm intent to prevent others from receiving the harvest.
Seeing the ruined garden confronts the owners with the collapse of their expectation.
They recognize that they have been deprived, directly reversing their assumed command of the garden.
The most balanced owner recalls their need to glorify God, like the companion's correction in 18:39.
The owners confess God's transcendence and their own wrongdoing after the garden's loss.
Their mutual blame records the social aftermath of a failed possessive scheme.
They admit their transgression, identifying moral failure within the loss of abundance.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better, directly echoing the believer's hope in 18:40.
The garden's punishment is stated as an earthly warning, with the greater final punishment beyond it.
The command to consider food opens a direct reflection on the source of agricultural provision.
Abundant poured water supplies the first stage of the crop-and-garden sequence.
The split earth supplies the prepared ground for divinely produced cultivation.
Grain is made to grow from the prepared earth.
Grapes and herbage are named among the produced provisions, directly echoing the garden imagery.
Olives and palm trees extend the catalogue of divinely grown orchard provision.
Thickly planted gardens are directly named as part of God's provision.
Fruit and pasture complete the agricultural system that sustains people and animals.
Excessive love of wealth gives a concise moral counterpart to the owner's boastful attachment.
Intense love of wealth is a direct inner disposition behind treating abundance as self-secured.
Competition for accumulation provides a concise social counterpart to boasting in wealth and followers.
